title: A DNS RR for specifying the location of services (DNS SRV)

hero.subtitle: Locating network services by name, protocol, and domain using DNS

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The SRV resource record allows administrators to specify the location of servers for a particular service and protocol using DNS. Instead of hard-coding server hostnames, clients can look up SRV records to discover which servers provide a service.

SRV records add load balancing and failover capabilities to DNS. By specifying priority and weight values, administrators can control how clients select among multiple servers.

The RFC says clients should use SRV only where the protocol specification for the application says they should. That specification must define the symbolic service name and include its own security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The SRV record lets a client ask DNS which servers provide a given service. Instead of hard-coding server names, clients look up SRV records, and priority and weight values let administrators balance load and set up backups. Clients should use SRV only where the application's own protocol specification says to.

sections.title: Format
sections.content:
An SRV record has the following name format and data fields:

SRV Record Name Format
_service._proto.name.  TTL  class  SRV  priority  weight  port  target

Example:
_http._tcp.example.com. 3600 IN SRV 10 60 80 www1.example.com.
_http._tcp.example.com. 3600 IN SRV 10 40 80 www2.example.com.
_http._tcp.example.com. 3600 IN SRV 20  0 80 backup.example.com.
_serviceSymbolic name of the service (e.g., _http, _sip, _ldap)Label
_protoTransport protocol: _tcp or _udpLabel
PriorityLower values are preferred; clients try lower priority first16 bits
WeightRelative weight for load balancing among same-priority servers16 bits
PortTCP or UDP port number for the service16 bits
TargetHostname of the server providing the serviceDomain name
sections.plainLanguage: An SRV record is named _service._proto.name, for example _http._tcp.example.com. Its data holds a priority, a weight, a port and the target host name. Lower priority values are preferred, and weight shares load among servers of equal priority.

sections.title: Usage
sections.content:
SRV records are widely used by modern protocols for service discovery:

_sip._tcpSIP — Voice over IP signaling
_xmpp-client._tcpXMPP — Jabber instant messaging
_ldap._tcpLDAP — Directory services
_kerberos._tcpKerberos — Authentication services
_minecraft._tcpMinecraft — Game server discovery

A target of "." (the root domain) means the service is explicitly not available at this domain. This is useful for declaring that a specific service is not offered.
sections.plainLanguage: Many protocols use SRV records to find servers, including SIP, XMPP, LDAP and Kerberos. A target of "." means the service is explicitly not available at that domain.

sections.title: Selection Algorithm
sections.content:
Clients use a two-level selection process to choose a server from SRV records:

Step 1: Sort by Priority
Group records by priority value. Always try the lowest-priority group first. Only move to the next priority group if all servers in the current group are unreachable.
Step 2: Weighted Selection
Within each priority group, select servers based on their weight. A server with weight 60 should receive roughly three times as many connections as a server with weight 20.
Weight Zero
Administrators SHOULD use weight 0 when there is no server selection to do. Among records that have weights greater than 0, a weight-0 record should have only a very small chance of being selected.

The RFC's algorithm for one priority level: list the unordered records with all weight-0 records first, compute a running sum of the weights, pick a uniform random number between 0 and the total (inclusive), and select the first record whose running sum is greater than or equal to that number. Remove it from the set and repeat until none remain.
sections.plainLanguage: A client picks a server in two steps. First it groups records by priority and tries the lowest value first, moving on only if every server in that group is unreachable. Within a group it chooses at random in proportion to weight, so weight 60 gets about three times the connections of weight 20. Weight 0 is used when there is no choice to make.

subtitle: Locating network services by name, protocol, and domain using DNS
summary: The DNS SRV record lets a client ask DNS where the servers for a given service and protocol in a domain are. A record named _service._proto.name carries a priority, a weight, a port and a target host, so administrators can run several servers, move them, and designate backups. Clients try the lowest priority first and pick among equals in proportion to weight.

plainLanguage.summary: The DNS SRV record lets a client ask DNS where the servers for a given service and protocol in a domain are. Each record carries a priority, a weight, a port and a target host. Clients try the lowest priority first and choose among equals in proportion to weight, so administrators can run several servers, move them and designate backups.

tldr.problem: To reach a server, a client had to know the server's host name, and translated service names to port numbers from local files such as /etc/services.
tldr.mechanism: A DNS SRV record named _service._proto.name lists priority, weight, port and target host; clients try the lowest priority first and choose among equals by weight.
tldr.outcome: Services can move between hosts, share load and have backups using only DNS, provided the application protocol says to use SRV.

today: SRV remains the standard way to find servers for protocols that call for it: SIP, XMPP and LDAP clients, Kerberos and many game and chat services look up _service._proto names. RFC 2782 itself says clients should use SRV only when the protocol specification says so. Web browsers have traditionally not used it for HTTP; RFC 9460 later defined SVCB and HTTPS records for similar service binding on the web.

data.title: SRV records for a SIP service
data.code:
_sip._tcp.example.com. 86400 IN SRV 10 60 5060 sip1.example.com.
_sip._tcp.example.com. 86400 IN SRV 10 20 5060 sip2.example.com.
_sip._tcp.example.com. 86400 IN SRV 20  0 5060 backup.example.com.

; Priority 10: sip1 (weight 60), sip2 (weight 20)
; Priority 20: backup (fallback)

fields.name: Priority
fields.desc: Lower is preferred. A client MUST attempt the lowest-numbered priority it can reach. Range 0-65535, 16-bit unsigned, network byte order.

fields.name: Weight
fields.desc: Relative weight among records of the same priority; larger weights SHOULD be selected proportionately more often. Range 0-65535.

fields.name: Port
fields.desc: Port on the target host for the service. Range 0-65535, often the Assigned Numbers value but need not be.

fields.name: Target
fields.desc: Domain name of the target host. Variable length, drawn here as one row. It MUST have address records, MUST NOT be an alias, and must not use name compression. "." means the service is not available.

data.title: The RFC's fictional "foobar" zone
data.code:
; foobar - use old-slow-box or new-fast-box if either is
; available, make three quarters of the logins go to
; new-fast-box.
_foobar._tcp    SRV 0 1 9 old-slow-box.example.com.
                SRV 0 3 9 new-fast-box.example.com.
; if neither old-slow-box or new-fast-box is up, switch to
; using the sysdmin's box and the server
                SRV 1 0 9 sysadmins-box.example.com.
                SRV 1 0 9 server.example.com.
; NO other services are supported
*._tcp          SRV 0 0 0 .
*._udp          SRV 0 0 0 .
